name: Shoulder Labral Tear and Instability
seo_title: Shoulder Labral Tear Treatment | Palm Beach Gardens, FL
seo_desc: Shoulder labral tear and instability care in Palm Beach Gardens and Port St. Lucie, from therapy to arthroscopic repair, by a board-certified surgeon.
lede: A shoulder that catches, clicks or feels like it could slip out may have a torn labrum, a common injury in throwing athletes and after dislocations.
what_it_is: The labrum is a firm rim of cartilage around the edge of your shoulder socket (the glenoid). According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, it deepens the socket by up to 50 percent and gives the stabilizing ligaments, along with one end of the biceps tendon, a place to attach. When the labrum tears, the ball of the upper arm bone sits less securely and may slip partway or fully out of the socket.

Tears are named by location. A SLAP tear involves the top of the labrum where the biceps attaches and is common in throwing athletes. A Bankart lesion sits at the front and bottom of the socket, usually after the ball dislocates forward. Posterior tears affect the back. Mayo Clinic notes that dislocations are most common in teens and people in their 20s, and that a prior dislocation raises the chance of another.
symptoms: A sense that the shoulder is loose or might slip out
Catching, locking, popping or grinding in the joint
Deep, aching pain with overhead activity or throwing
Reduced strength and range of motion
Repeated episodes of the shoulder giving out or dislocating
causes: A direct blow to the shoulder or a sudden pull on the arm
Repetitive overhead motion in throwing sports and weightlifting
Contact and collision sports such as football and hockey

how_therapy_helps.intro: Not every labral tear needs an operation. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists physical therapy as first-line care, with bracing for some unstable shoulders, and its instability guidance centers on physical therapy that strengthens the shoulder muscles and improves shoulder control. Surgery is considered when pain, catching or repeated dislocations continue. Dr. Matarazzo weighs your age, your sport and how many times the shoulder has come out when helping you choose between the two.
methods: A guided program strengthens the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles so they keep the ball centered in the socket, backed by exercises you continue at home.
Pausing throwing, overhead lifting and contact play while pain settles, with NSAIDs if they are safe for you, reduces repeated stress on the torn rim.
For some instability, AAOS notes a brace can help by limiting the arm positions that let the shoulder slip.
Through small incisions, the torn labrum is reattached to the socket rim with suture anchors. This is typically a same-day outpatient procedure.
Some instability cases are better suited to an open procedure through a shoulder incision, which lets the surgeon see and repair the structures directly.

first_visit: Dr. Matarazzo asks how the problem began, whether the shoulder has ever come out of place and how often, and what sports or work you do. The exam checks how loose the joint is, which arm positions bring on pain or a feeling of slipping, and your strength and motion. X-rays look for bone injury. An MRI, sometimes with contrast dye (an arthrogram), shows the labrum best, and a CT scan can measure bone loss after repeat dislocations.
recovery: With therapy alone, results depend on how well stronger muscles control the joint, and Mayo Clinic notes a shoulder that has dislocated carries a higher risk of doing so again. After arthroscopic labral repair, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says to expect a sling for 2 to 6 weeks and limits on lifting for about 12 weeks, with the shoulder fully healed in 4 to 6 months. When you return to throwing or contact sport is decided with your surgeon and therapist based on strength, motion and the demands of your sport.
self_care: Avoid the arm positions that make the shoulder feel unstable, often reaching overhead or out to the side and back.
Hold off on throwing, overhead lifting and contact sports until you have been evaluated.
Use a cold pack for up to 20 minutes at a time to ease soreness after activity.
Keep moving the shoulder gently in comfortable ranges so it does not stiffen.
see_a_doctor: A shoulder that looks out of place or misshapen after a fall or hit: go to an emergency room or urgent care, and do not try to pop it back in
Numbness, tingling or weakness in the arm after an injury
An arm that feels unusually hot or cold, or is badly swollen
Repeated episodes of the shoulder giving out
Catching or locking that keeps returning and limits your activity

faqs.q: Can a torn labrum in the shoulder heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Many people manage a labral tear without surgery. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists physical therapy to rebuild strength and motion as the first step, with bracing for some unstable shoulders. Therapy does not reattach the torn tissue, but stronger muscles can control the joint well enough to quiet symptoms. Surgery is usually considered when pain, catching or instability continue despite a full course of rehab.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a SLAP tear and a Bankart tear?
faqs.a: Both are tears of the shoulder labrum, named for where they occur. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, a SLAP tear is at the top of the socket where the biceps tendon attaches and is common in throwing athletes. A Bankart tear is at the front lower edge of the socket and usually follows a forward shoulder dislocation. Location guides both the exam findings and the treatment plan.

It might. Mayo Clinic notes that once a shoulder has dislocated, the risk of another dislocation rises, especially after a severe injury, and that dislocations are most common in teens and people in their 20s. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons explains that a forward dislocation often tears the front of the labrum, leaving the joint looser. Strengthening helps, and surgery is an option if the shoulder keeps slipping.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI for a labral tear?
faqs.a: X-rays show bone, so they cannot reveal a torn labrum, which is soft tissue. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, MRI is the best imaging choice for labral injuries, and an MR arthrogram, where contrast dye is injected into the joint first, can reveal subtle tears. Your surgeon decides whether imaging is needed based on your exam and how your shoulder responds to early treatment.

faqs.q: Is arthroscopic or open surgery better for shoulder instability?
faqs.a: Both approaches are used. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, arthroscopy repairs the labrum and ligaments through tiny incisions with a small camera and is usually a same-day outpatient procedure. Open surgery uses a larger incision so the surgeon can work on the structures directly. Either way, recovery involves time in a sling followed by progressive motion and strengthening. The right choice depends on the specific damage in your shoulder.

faqs.q: Can you tear your shoulder labrum without dislocating it?
faqs.a: Yes. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that labral tears can come from a fall on an outstretched arm, a direct blow, a sudden pull on the arm, or repetitive shoulder motion in throwing athletes and weightlifters. Some posterior tears develop from gradual wear. In these cases the shoulder may hurt, click or catch without ever fully coming out of the socket.
